heading_ja: 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ付き）（cl-23）

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in jukugo-ruby character complex. — JA: どの文字も熟語ルビのルビ付きの親文字群の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: § A.23 has no table and no Remarks column: its whole text is the one sentence quoted above, in each locale. That sentence is a license rather than a list, so this class has no key to look up — no code point is a member and none is excluded, and the only question a case can ask is about a construct. This case therefore states the class over the ruby (ルビ) construct the caller declared. The two base characters are the ideographic characters (cl-19) of a kanji compound word (熟語, jukugo) and each carries two ruby characters, which is § 3.3.7's first paragraph and not its second, so the construct is a jukugo-ruby complex by the specification's own description of one. The occurrence asked about is the first base; its own Appendix A key is a CJK Unified Ideograph and would answer cl-19 with no construct declared, which is the twin case below. § 3.3.7's Note is why cl-23 rather than cl-19 has to be the answer: it says the complexes of base characters with ruby characters "are classified as simple-ruby character complex (cl-22) and jukugo-ruby character complex (cl-23)" and that their handling with adjacent characters is published in § B "as a complete table in accordance with § 3.9 About Character Classes", so a base answering cl-19 leaves every cl-23 row and column of that table unreachable and § B.2 note 11, § C.2 note 8 and § E.2 note 7 dead letters. The case names no writing direction, so the direction-parity gate runs it both ways: cl-23 membership is not direction-conditional, and § 3.3.4's choice of the side the ruby is attached to is a property of where the annotation is placed rather than of what class the base is in.

forbidden.why: Answering the occurrence's own Appendix A key and ignoring the construct it sits in. § 3.3.7's Note routes these complexes to § B's table 'in accordance with § 3.9 About Character Classes', and § B.2 note 11 and § C.2 note 8 both index on cl-23, so a base that answers cl-19 makes those notes unreachable. § A.23 is also not a subset of Appendix A's frame: the preamble scopes the appendix to 'lists of (non-ideographic) characters from a subset of ISO/IEC 10646', and § A.23 states a license over every character instead of listing any, so the absence of a table is not the absence of members.

Collapsing the two ruby complexes into one class. § 3.9.2 names them separately — 'Simple-ruby character complexes (cl-22)' / 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22） against 'Jukugo-ruby character complexes (cl-23)' / 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ付き）（cl-23） — and the Japanese names differ by exactly 熟語ルビ以外 against 熟語ルビ. § B.2 notes 10 and 11 and § C.2 notes 7 and 8 then state different rules for the two, and § C.2 note 8 is the only complex note in the document that puts a line break opportunity inside one complex.

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in jukugo-ruby character complex. — JA: どの文字も熟語ルビのルビ付きの親文字群の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: The same input, asked at the second base. It is worth a case of its own because a jukugo-ruby complex is the one construct in the document whose interior is subdivided: § 3.3.7 pairs each base character with its own run of ruby text, and § C.2 note 8 puts a line break opportunity at the seam between one such pair and the next. An implementation that models the complex as a single indivisible unit — which is what § C.2 notes 6 and 7 require of cl-21 and cl-22 — can still answer the first base correctly and lose the second, or answer the second from the first's run. Membership does not stop at a run boundary: § A.23's sentence is about the complex, and § 3.9.2's Note under cl-21 defines 親文字群 (base characters complex) as 'characters in a complex including ruby, ornament characters and emphasis dots', which is the whole of it. So both bases are cl-23 and the run pairing, which this input states as data because § B.2 notes 9 to 11 and § C.2 notes 6 to 8 all turn on it, changes nothing about the class.

cases.quote: The following are lists of (non-ideographic) characters from a subset of ISO/IEC 10646 (collection number 285 "BASIC JAPANESE" and 286 "JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION") grouped by character class according to the classification explained in § 3.9.2 Grouping of Characters and Symbols depending on their Positioning.
cases.rationale: The differential twin of the first case and the whole assertion of this file. The text, the items, the scales and the frames are byte-identical; the ruby construct and its annotation stream are removed and nothing else changes; and the answer changes from cl-23 to cl-19. That pair is what it means for cl-23 to be a property of an occurrence rather than of a code point (ADR 0008): the two bases here are the same two CJK Unified Ideographs, so no lookup keyed on the character can produce both answers, and an implementation that reaches cl-23 through a table of code points has either made every ideograph a cl-23 member or made none. The quoted preamble is why the answer here is cl-19 and not cl-23 by default: Appendix A is a set of lists over a bounded subset of ISO/IEC 10646, § A.19 states that its own table is that class's non-ideographic complement, and an occurrence in no construct falls to the class its key names. It is also why the absence of a table under § A.23 must not be read the other way — as 'no member of the subset is in cl-23' — since § A.23 answers with a license instead of participating in the frame the preamble sets up.

forbidden.why: Reading § A.23's 'any character' as an unconditional membership. The sentence licenses every character to participate in a jukugo-ruby character complex; it says nothing about a character that is in none. If it did, every one of the thirty classes would hold every character, since § A.20 to § A.23 and § A.30 state the same sentence about five different constructs, and § 3.9.2's grouping would carry no information at all.

cases.quote: EN: The name of this class in JIS X 4051 is "Characters included in base characters complex with jukugo-ruby". — JA: JIS X 4051の名称は，“熟語ルビ付き親文字群中の文字”である．
cases.rationale: The second differential twin, and the boundary the document draws between cl-22 and cl-23. Everything is byte-identical to the first case except the ruby style, which is declared mono (モノルビ) rather than jukugo, and the answer is cl-22. The two classes are distinguished by nothing else: § 3.9.2 names them 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ以外のルビ付き）（cl-22） and 親文字群中の文字（熟語ルビ付き）（cl-23）, which differ by the four characters 熟語ルビ以外 against 熟語ルビ, and the quoted Note gives cl-23 the JIS X 4051 name 'Characters included in base characters complex with jukugo-ruby' against cl-22's 'Characters included in base characters complex with ruby (excluding jukugo-ruby)'. § 3.3.4's closing paragraph names the three composition methods the sections after it explain — mono-ruby, group-ruby and jukugo-ruby, モノルビ，グループルビ及び熟語ルビ, one each to § 3.3.5, § 3.3.6 and § 3.3.7 — so 'excluding jukugo-ruby' is the other two, and mono-ruby over the same two bases with the same reading is a cl-22 complex. The two cases are worth publishing as a pair because the caller's declared style is the only input that separates them, which is exactly the shape of § B.2 notes 10 and 11 and of § C.2 notes 7 and 8: same geometry, different rule.

forbidden.why: Answering cl-23 for any base carrying ruby. § 3.3.7's Note splits the ruby complexes into cl-22 and cl-23 and hands both to § B's table; § C.2 note 7 forbids a line break anywhere inside a cl-22 complex while § C.2 note 8 puts one between each base and the next inside a cl-23 complex. An implementation that answers cl-23 here breaks a mono-ruby complex across two lines at a seam § C.2 note 7 closes.

cases.quote: EN: The meaning of "base characters complex" is characters in a complex including ruby, ornament characters and emphasis dots. — JA: 親文字群とは，親文字及びそれに付随するルビ，添え字又は圏点を含めた文字群のことである．
cases.rationale: The near miss: a character that sits immediately after a jukugo-ruby complex, that the complex's ruby may be allowed to hang over, and that is not a member of cl-23. The quoted Note is stated once, under cl-21 in § 3.9.2, and governs cl-22 and cl-23 through the shared name 親文字群; it bounds the complex at the base characters together with the ruby, ornament characters or emphasis dots attached to *them*. A neighbor carries none of those, so it is outside, and its own key answers — katakana (cl-16) here. § B.2 note 7 says the same thing from the other side, by naming a cl-22 or cl-23 complex 'adjacent to katakana (cl-16)': the katakana whose space the ruby borrows is still cl-16 while it is being overhung, or the note could not name it. The occurrence asked about is the first katakana after the complex, which is the position where an implementation that grows the complex outward to whatever the ruby reaches would answer differently.

forbidden.why: Extending the complex to whatever its ruby overhangs. § 3.9.2's Note under cl-21 bounds 親文字群 at the base characters and the ruby, ornament characters or emphasis dots attached to them, and this occurrence carries none. If a character the ruby hangs over were a member, § B.2 note 7 could not state its rule: it is about a cl-22 or cl-23 complex adjacent to katakana (cl-16), and that adjacency would be a cl-23 pair instead, which § B.2 note 11 already answers with a different rule.

cases.quote: The character advance of commas (cl-07), full stops (cl-06), opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and middle dots (cl-05) is half-width (half em).
cases.rationale: The second near miss, and the one place a frame (字幅) matters anywhere near this class. § A.23 has no Remarks column, so no frame separates a cl-23 answer from anything — the frame axis is empty for this class. It is not empty for its neighbors: § 3.1.2 states an advance for five classes, so the opening bracket and the closing bracket here must declare a frame or the stream is malformed, and they declare the half em frame § 3.1.2 states. The occurrence asked about is the opening bracket, which § B.2 note 1 pairs with a cl-22 or cl-23 complex — 'When opening brackets (cl-01) are followed by a simple-ruby character complex (cl-22) or jukugo-ruby character complex (cl-23)' — and that pairing is the evidence that the bracket is the complex's neighbor rather than one of its members, since a rule about a boundary between two things needs both of them. So the answer is cl-01, and it is the same cl-01 it would be with no ruby anywhere: the construct axis and the frame axis are independent, and declaring a ruby construct over the two characters between the brackets moves neither bracket into cl-23.

forbidden.why: Reading § B.2 note 1's overhang permission as membership. The note lets the ruby of a following cl-22 or cl-23 complex extend over the opening bracket; it names the bracket as cl-01 while doing so, and a boundary rule between cl-01 and cl-23 cannot be stated if the cl-01 side is also cl-23.

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in jukugo-ruby character complex. — JA: どの文字も熟語ルビのルビ付きの親文字群の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: Two jukugo-ruby complexes set side by side, with the question asked at the first base of the second one. The class is cl-23 on both sides of that seam, which is the point: the class does not distinguish one complex from another, and every rule the document states about the seam does. § B.2 note 11 sets two adjacent characters of *different* jukugo-ruby complexes solid and hands two of the *same* complex to § 3.3.7; § C.2 note 8 puts a line break opportunity between two bases of different complexes; § E.2 note 7 puts a third-order expansion opportunity of up to a quarter em there and nowhere else in or around one. All three read a complex identity that the class cannot carry, which is why this input declares two entries in `constructs.ruby` rather than one construct with four bases, and why a report names a construct by its kind and its position in that array. An implementation that merges adjacent complexes because their bases are contiguous and their class is equal answers this case correctly and then loses all three rules at once.

cases.quote: EN: If there is any ideographic character (cl-19) in a given kanji compound word which needs three or more ruby characters, the jukugo-ruby layout cannot be used. In this case, attach the ruby text to the kanji compound word as a whole. — JA: 熟語を構成するそれぞれの漢字等（cl-19）の中で，1字でもそれに対応するルビ文字が3字以上のものがある場合，熟語全体とルビ文字の文字列を対応させて配置する．
cases.rationale: The only boundary § 3.3.7 draws around a jukugo-ruby construct, and the two renderings of that sentence do not draw it in the same place. The base characters are the document's own example: § 3.1.10's Note names 哺 with ほ, 乳 with にゆう and 類 with るい as a jukugo-ruby (熟語ルビ) that may be divided between one base-and-its-ruby group and the next, and the middle base carries three ruby characters. This file writes the middle reading にゅう with the small ゅ where § 3.1.10's Note prints にゆう with the full-size ゆ; either spelling is three ruby characters, which is the quantity § 3.3.7 keys on, so the count the case turns on is unchanged. The English half then says that for exactly this compound 'the jukugo-ruby layout cannot be used'; the Japanese half says only that the whole compound is set against the whole reading, and § 3.3.7's own Note calls the one-plus-three pattern a jukugo-ruby that is often met and would be ugly as mono-ruby. So JLReq states the class two ways and this project adjudicates rather than pretending it states one. The two readings are keyed on the question § 3.3.7 itself opens. Under the JIS X 4051 method, which § 3.3.7 calls 'similar to the group-ruby method described in § 3.3.6', the reading is distributed over the compound exactly as group-ruby is, and cl-22's own JIS name is 'Characters included in base characters complex with ruby (excluding jukugo-ruby)' — so that choice reads with the English half and answers cl-22. Under the other method, whose detail § 3.3.7 hands to an appendix headed 'Positioning of Jukugo-ruby', the complex is still positioned as jukugo-ruby, and that choice reads with the Japanese half and answers cl-23. Neither answer is licensed by the specification alone, which is what the standing above records.

permitted.source: JLReq Japanese half of 3.3.7, with 3.3.7's own Note on the one-plus-three pattern and 3.1.10's Note naming this compound a jukugo-ruby: the complex stays cl-23

JLReq English half of 3.3.7 ('the jukugo-ruby layout cannot be used') with the JIS X 4051 method 3.3.7 calls similar to group-ruby (3.3.6), which is A.22's ruby excluding jukugo-ruby: the complex is cl-22

forbidden.why: Falling back to the base's own key because § 3.3.7 withdrew a layout. The sentence withdraws a positioning method, not the complex: the ruby is still attached, § 3.3.7 says in both locales what to do instead, and § 3.9.2's Note under cl-21 makes a base with ruby attached a member of a 親文字群 whichever method places it. Whether that complex is cl-22 or cl-23 is what the two entries above record; that it is neither is what no reading of § 3.3.7 supports.
